doc.title: Dawoud Sabu Adeyola interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 30, 2025

title: Miles Davis quintet at the Town Casino, New Year's 1963
summary: Listening as a bassist, record collection in Germany, and seeing the young Miles Davis quintet to a small audience.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: Did you get the impression, once you started playing the bass, I’m going to guess that your listening habits started centering more on that part of the music and you start to learn patterns and hearing them before you even went to play them.

Yes. Yeah absolutely. I had — when I was in Germany, when I first started in Germany I had a bunch of records. We had what they call a BX or base exchange that had a lot of records. It had a nice record selection. And so I wound up with a couple of hundred albums in my room in the barracks you know. And another early experience that affected my whole life was New Year’s Eve 1963. I was going into my — well actually I was in the middle of my senior year. Because I graduated in June of ’64. So yeah it was my junior year. ’63 was coming in and Miles Davis came to — the Miles Davis Quintet came to downtown Buffalo. I think it was the Town Casino. And I had been listening to the records, those records he made on Prestige, before he got to Columbia you know, he made a bunch of records just to get out of the contract. “Relaxin’ with the Miles Davis Quartet,” “Workin’ with the Miles Davis Quintet,” “Cookin’ with the Miles Davis Quartet,” and even beyond — even before that when he was making records with Bird and “Birth of the Cool.” But I was really into what they call hard bop with most of those groups that had John Coltrane, Paul Chambers, Red Garland. So anyway, when I heard he was coming to the Town Casino of course I showed up. And — but I was disappointed when I got there because I was looking for Paul Chambers, Wynton Kelly or Red Garland. And maybe Coltrane or somebody like that. He shown in with these new guys you know, that I had never heard of before. These young guys. Tony Williams, you know, Ron Carter, Herbie Hancock.
He couldn’t get anybody good, huh?

And George Coleman. And I’m like oh man, that Miles, come on man, what are you doing man, who are these guys? Not realizing that this is the group that going to be called the second great quintet. And so that’s what I remember about that concert, that I was very disappointed at first, but then when I heard them I said, well yeah, this might be okay — he had just put that group together — and the other thing I remember about that concert is how small the audience was. I was like where’s everybody? I mean what? This is Miles Davis. I mean even a kid of sixteen, you know, in those days and I’m saying this place is supposed to be packed. But at least the night I went he think I had about two or three nights, and the night I went there was almost no one there.
Do you recall, beyond the music, noticing how they operate on stage? Visual cues, just watching the bass player interact with the drummer, was any of that apparent to you? © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

Oh yeah, yeah. I was very — especially I mean the first concert, I mean with the Cannonball thing and George Shearing, — Kleinhans — you know I’m sitting way in the back and you know I couldn’t really focus in on the interactions and that, but at the Town Casino I’m sitting right almost underneath him you know and I could see. And then of course everybody had an eye on Miles ‘cause he had a reputation for doing different stuff, turning his back or leaving the stage, you know and that kind of stuff you know. And so I’m really watching him. And this time I had no idea about music as a profession or bass or anything like that, I’m just really somebody who fell in love with the music and was kind of trying to follow it you know. But they were definitely communicating with each other, but again, not to the extent that they got to later on you know I mean because I think he announced that this group was brand new, only, not even six months old. And so they were still kind of feeling each other out, you know what I mean? To play with each other. And I think that was in the time with Tony, they had to paint a moustache on him to try to get him in because he was only — he was under-aged. You know.
He wasn’t that much older than you at the time, was he?
One year. One year. I think he was born in ’46, I was born in ‘ 47.
